summary: Specifies how the reserved bits in the PIM common header may be used by message types and extends the PIM type space. It updates several PIM-related RFCs.

eli5.summary: A message header had spare bits. This says how they may be used, and makes room for more message types.

questions: how many pim message types are there
subtitle: Gives the spare bits in the PIM message header a job and makes room for 48 new PIM message types.

tldr.problem: All PIM version 2 messages share a common header with eight reserved bits, but no document formally said how individual message types may use them, and the type space was running low.
tldr.mechanism: The reserved field is renamed the Flag Bits field and is defined per message type. Types 13, 14 and 15 each gain a 4-bit Subtype taken from the flag bits, giving 48 extended types.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 8736, updates six other PIM specifications and updates the IANA PIM Message Types registry.

today: RFC 9436 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 8736 and updates RFC 3973, RFC 5015, RFC 5059, RFC 6754, RFC 7761 and RFC 8364. No later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
PIM version 2 messages share a common header defined in the PIM Sparse Mode specification, RFC 7761. That header contains eight reserved bits, but no document formally specified that these bits are to be used per message type.

RFC 9436 renames the Reserved field the Flag Bits field and says the bits are used separately for each message type. The originally defined message types ran from 0 to 15, and type 15 had been reserved by RFC 6166 for type space extension. This document obsoletes RFC 8736, which had made the RFC 6166 extension obsolete.
sections.eli5: A form had some blank boxes nobody had rules for. This document says who may write in which box.

sections.title: The Common Header and Flag Bits
sections.content:
The updated common header has a PIM version field, a Type field, the Flag Bits field and a Checksum. All fields other than Flag Bits remain unchanged.

Unless a message type says otherwise, its flag bits are Unassigned: they MUST be set to zero on transmission and MUST be ignored on receipt. A new PIM type MUST say whether its bits are treated differently. Bits are numbered from bit 7, the most significant and immediately after the Type field, down to bit 0, right before the Checksum.
sections.eli5: Each blank box is numbered. If no rule says what a box is for, you leave it empty and ignore anything someone puts in it.

sections.title: Flag Bits in Existing Message Types
sections.content:
The document records how three existing message types already use the bits.

  • Type 4 (Bootstrap) defines bit 7 as No-Forward; the other bits are unassigned.
  • Type 10 (DF Election) uses the four most significant bits (bits 4 to 7) as a subtype; the rest are unassigned.
  • Type 12 (PIM Flooding Mechanism) defines bit 7 as No-Forward; the rest are unassigned.

Each usage is defined in the document that specifies that message type.
sections.eli5: Three kinds of messages already had a use for some boxes. This document just writes that down in one place.

sections.title: Extending the Type Space
sections.content:
Types 13, 14 and 15 each become 16 new types, for 48 types available to future PIM extensions. This is done with a Subtype field made from the four most significant flag bits (bits 4 to 7). The notation type.subtype, such as 13.0, names an extended type. The remaining four flag bits (bits 0 to 3) are defined by each extended type.

An extended type is the eight bits made by joining Type and Subtype. No relationship is expected or implied between extended types that share a Type value.
sections.eli5: Three kinds of labels each get sixteen sub-labels, like three shelves each split into sixteen boxes, so there is room for many new message kinds.

sections.title: Registry Changes and Security
sections.content:
The IANA "PIM Message Types" registry is updated to show which flag bits each type uses, with bits unassigned except where already specified. The registration policy stays IETF Review, and new assignments MUST define any non-default flag bit usage. Extended type 15.15 is Reserved for future extensions, and new extended types should be assigned consecutively starting with 13.0, then 13.1. IANA also changed references to RFC 8736 in the registry to point to RFC 9436.

On security, the document says it only clarifies flag bit use and extends the type space, so it has no impact on security and does not change the considerations in RFC 7761 and RFC 3973.
sections.eli5: The official list of message types was updated. The last slot is kept empty on purpose, and new ones are handed out in order. Nothing about safety changes.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: Message type; 13, 14 or 15 for extended types.

fields.name: Subtype
fields.desc: Flag bits 4 to 7, selecting one of 16 subtypes.

fields.name: FB
fields.desc: Flag bits 0 to 3, defined by each extended type.
